papers.title: Phenotype-structured nonlocal aggregation models I: signal production and response
papers.summary: Individuals within a cellular or ecological population can exhibit substantial variation in their traits or phenotype. Such heterogeneity can fundamentally alter population-level behaviour, including the ability to aggregate and form spatial patterns. We investigate these effects by extending nonlocal aggregation models, widely used to model cell--cell adhesion and collective animal movement, to incorporate phenotype structure. We characterise how heterogeneity and switching between phenotypes affect whether patterns form, how phenotypes are distributed within them, and whether they are stationary or exhibit spatio-temporal oscillations. We show that pattern formation is promoted when phenotypes that produce stronger interaction signals also respond more strongly to them, whereas specialisation towards either signal production or response inhibits pattern formation. Increasing rates of switching between phenotypes dampen these effects. Heterogeneity can also enable weakly interacting, and even repulsive, individuals to pattern as part of the collective. Furthermore, movement in phenotype and physical space can interact to restructure patterns and generate spatio-temporal oscillations. A further key message of this study is the value of considering both discrete $N$-phenotype and continuous phenotype formulations. We develop both in parallel, demonstrating formal correspondences, but also advantages to each framework in terms of mathematical analyses and interpretability.

papers.title: Collision Dynamics of Topologically Pumped Solitons
papers.summary: Soliton pumping enables controlled transport of localized wave packets through the interplay between nonlinearity and band topology. Interactions between such wave packets provide an additional means to manipulate their localization and subsequent motion. Here, we investigate collisions of solitons in a driven bichromatic lattice, where solitons associated with bands of opposite Chern numbers are pumped toward one another. For intracomponent collisions, the soliton that dominates the collision survives as a localized outgoing wave packet, while the weaker one can lose its distinct localized identity. For intercomponent collisions, attractive interaction produces spatial locking, whereas repulsive interaction induces redistribution toward the lowest band and reverses the motion of the initially excited-band wave packet. Remarkably, for collisions between vector solitons with comparable initial intensities, the difference between their internal relative phases controls the collision outcome, favoring capture for in-phase preparation and re-separation for out-of-phase preparation. These results connect nonlinear scattering with subsequent topological pumping and identify initial intensity, intercomponent interaction, and relative phase as control parameters for manipulating localized transport within the same pumping protocol.
